title: Replication and consistency
summary: Say what a replica is for and what a client can see after a write.

parts.rule: Replication keeps copies of data for read capacity, failover, or geographic proximity. State who accepts writes, whether acknowledgement waits for replicas, and what a read may observe. Asynchronous replicas can lag; synchronous acknowledgement adds write latency. Match each user path to a consistency guarantee such as eventual, bounded-stale, read-your-writes, or strong.
parts.why: Adding replicas changes behavior, not just capacity. A successful write may be absent from a replica for milliseconds or seconds, and a failover may lose acknowledged writes that had not copied. Without an explicit read rule, users can refresh and appear to lose their own update. Without fencing, an old primary can return and create two writers.
parts.example: A comments service has one primary and 3 asynchronous read replicas. User 42 creates comment 91. The primary commits it at log position 10,042 and returns 201, while a replica is still at 10,038 with about 200 ms of lag. If the next GET /comments is routed there, comment 91 is missing. To provide read-your-writes, keep user 42 on the primary briefly or return the commit position and route the read only to a replica that has replayed at least 10,042. Other readers may accept the 200 ms delay, so their feed reads can use any healthy replica. For a balance transfer, route the authoritative balance read to the primary or a store offering the required strong semantics; “there are replicas” is not enough. During failover, promote the most up-to-date eligible replica and fence the old primary before accepting new writes. With asynchronous replication, acknowledge that the last unreplicated commits may be lost. Waiting for one synchronous standby lowers that risk but adds a network round trip and can reduce write availability when the standby is unreachable. Replication also copies accidental deletes, so backups and point-in-time recovery remain separate requirements.
parts.use: Add replicas when measured read traffic, availability, or regional latency requires them. Put the consistency choice beside each read path and monitor replication lag. Define failover selection, old-primary fencing, and the recovery point objective before claiming that replicas improve availability.
parts.refuse: Do not promise zero acknowledged-write loss with ordinary asynchronous replication. Avoid sending all reads to replicas when a workflow requires current data, but also avoid sending every read to the primary after adding replicas for scale. Multi-primary designs require a concrete conflict policy. Replicas are not backups and do not replace recovery testing.

body:
Rule. Replication keeps copies of data for read capacity, failover, or geographic proximity. State who accepts writes, whether acknowledgement waits for replicas, and what a read may observe. Asynchronous replicas can lag; synchronous acknowledgement adds write latency. Match each user path to a consistency guarantee such as eventual, bounded-stale, read-your-writes, or strong.

Why it matters. Adding replicas changes behavior, not just capacity. A successful write may be absent from a replica for milliseconds or seconds, and a failover may lose acknowledged writes that had not copied. Without an explicit read rule, users can refresh and appear to lose their own update. Without fencing, an old primary can return and create two writers.

Worked example. A comments service has one primary and 3 asynchronous read replicas. User 42 creates comment 91. The primary commits it at log position 10,042 and returns 201, while a replica is still at 10,038 with about 200 ms of lag. If the next GET /comments is routed there, comment 91 is missing. To provide read-your-writes, keep user 42 on the primary briefly or return the commit position and route the read only to a replica that has replayed at least 10,042. Other readers may accept the 200 ms delay, so their feed reads can use any healthy replica. For a balance transfer, route the authoritative balance read to the primary or a store offering the required strong semantics; “there are replicas” is not enough. During failover, promote the most up-to-date eligible replica and fence the old primary before accepting new writes. With asynchronous replication, acknowledge that the last unreplicated commits may be lost. Waiting for one synchronous standby lowers that risk but adds a network round trip and can reduce write availability when the standby is unreachable. Replication also copies accidental deletes, so backups and point-in-time recovery remain separate requirements.

[[diagram:replica]]

When to use. Add replicas when measured read traffic, availability, or regional latency requires them. Put the consistency choice beside each read path and monitor replication lag. Define failover selection, old-primary fencing, and the recovery point objective before claiming that replicas improve availability.

When to refuse. Do not promise zero acknowledged-write loss with ordinary asynchronous replication. Avoid sending all reads to replicas when a workflow requires current data, but also avoid sending every read to the primary after adding replicas for scale. Multi-primary designs require a concrete conflict policy. Replicas are not backups and do not replace recovery testing.
